# Mathematical and Physical Foundations for Systems Engineers {.unnumbered}

This appendix provides a self-contained, systems-oriented reference for the mathematical and control-theoretic formulations used across this book. 

For systems, embedded, and software engineers, mathematical formulas in Physical AI are not abstract analytical exercises; they are the **specifications for real-time silicon execution**. Every equation maps directly into memory access patterns, execution cycle budgets ($\text{WCET}$), numerical precision requirements, and physical safety bounds.

---

## 1. Kinematics, Stopping Envelopes, and Reaction Debt

### The Physical Derivation of Stopping Distance
When an embodied robot maneuvers at linear velocity $v(t)$, the distance required to bring its physical mass to a complete, controlled stop consists of two decoupled components:

1. **Reaction Drift ($d_{\text{drift}}$):** The distance traversed while sensory signals propagate through transduction, bus serialization, neural inference, and communication queues before the actuators can apply braking torque.
2. **Kinematic Braking ($d_{\text{brake}}$):** The distance traversed while physical friction or counter-electromotive braking forces decelerate the moving mass at maximum safe deceleration $a_{\text{max}}$.

```
|<----------------------- Total Stopping Distance d_stop ------------------------>|
|                                                |                                 |
|  Reaction Drift (d_drift = v * tau_latency)    |  Kinematic Braking (v^2 / 2a)   |
|===============================================>|================================>|
t = 0 (Hazard Appears)                     t = tau (Brakes Engage)          t = t_stop (V=0)
```

Integrating Newtonian dynamics under constant deceleration $a(t) = -a_{\text{max}}$:

$$v(t) = v_0 - a_{\text{max}} t \implies t_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v_0}{a_{\text{max}}}$$

$$d_{\text{brake}} = \int_0^{t_{\text{brake}}} (v_0 - a_{\text{max}} t) \, dt = v_0 t_{\text{brake}} - \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{max}} t_{\text{brake}}^2 = \frac{v_0^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}$$

Accounting for total sensorimotor transport latency $\tau_{\text{latency}}$, the **Total Dynamic Stopping Envelope** is:

$$d_{\text{stop}}(v) = \underbrace{v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}}}_{\text{Reaction Drift}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}}_{\text{Kinematic Braking}}$$

where:
* $v$: Current operational velocity ($\text{m/s}$).
* $\tau_{\text{latency}}$: Total end-to-end transport delay ($\text{s}$), encompassing camera exposure, bus serialization (CAN-FD/PCIe), operating system scheduling tail latency, and inverter current rise time.
* $a_{\text{max}}$: Maximum permissible physical braking deceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$), constrained by tire friction coefficient ($\mu g$), payload tipping limits, or motor peak torque.

### Parabolic Safe Velocity Clamping
Given a measured physical clearance $d_{\text{clearance}}$ to an obstacle and a safety margin $d_{\text{margin}}$, the maximum safe operational velocity $v_{\text{safe}}$ is derived by solving the quadratic inequality $d_{\text{stop}}(v) \le d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}}$:

$$\frac{1}{2 a_{\text{max}}} v^2 + \tau_{\text{latency}} v - (d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}}) \le 0$$

Applying the quadratic formula and selecting the positive root:

$$v_{\text{safe}} = \sqrt{a_{\text{max}}^2 \tau_{\text{latency}}^2 + 2 a_{\text{max}} (d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}})} - a_{\text{max}} \tau_{\text{latency}}$$

### Embedded C Implementation
In real-time firmware, this check executes at $1000\text{ Hz}$ in static SRAM with zero dynamic memory allocation:

```c
#include <math.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef struct {
    float tau_latency_s;  // Total sensorimotor delay (e.g., 0.025 s)
    float a_max_mps2;     // Max braking deceleration (e.g., 2.5 m/s^2)
    float d_margin_m;     // Safety margin buffer (e.g., 0.15 m)
} stopping_params_t;

// Compute stopping distance in meters (WCET <= 1.2 microseconds on Cortex-M7)
float compute_stopping_distance(float v_mps, const stopping_params_t* params) {
    if (v_mps <= 0.0f) return 0.0f;
    float d_drift = v_mps * params->tau_latency_s;
    float d_brake = (v_mps * v_mps) / (2.0f * params->a_max_mps2);
    return d_drift + d_brake;
}

// Compute safe velocity clamp in m/s
float compute_safe_velocity_clamp(float d_clearance_m, const stopping_params_t* params) {
    float effective_clearance = d_clearance_m - params->d_margin_m;
    if (effective_clearance <= 0.0f) return 0.0f;
    
    float a = params->a_max_mps2;
    float tau = params->tau_latency_s;
    float discriminant = (a * a * tau * tau) + (2.0f * a * effective_clearance);
    
    return sqrtf(discriminant) - (a * tau);
}
```

## 2. Spatial Transformations: $SE(3)$, Quaternions, and Tangent Space $\mathfrak{se}(3)$

Physical AI agents operate in three-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$. To transform sensor observations, object affordances, and robot kinematics across coordinate frames, systems rely on the Special Euclidean Group $SE(3)$.

### Homogeneous Transformation Matrices
A rigid-body transformation from coordinate frame $A$ to coordinate frame $B$ consists of a 3D rotation $\mathbf{R}_A^B \in SO(3)$ and a 3D translation $\mathbf{p}_A^B \in \mathbb{R}^3$, unified into a $4 \times 4$ homogeneous matrix $\mathbf{T}_A^B \in SE(3)$:

$$\mathbf{T}_A^B = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_A^B & \mathbf{p}_A^B \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}$$

Points in 3D space are transformed using homogeneous coordinates $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = [\mathbf{x}^T, 1]^T$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_B = \mathbf{T}_A^B \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_A \implies \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_B \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_A^B \mathbf{x}_A + \mathbf{p}_A^B \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Matrix inversion in $SE(3)$ has a closed-form structure that avoids general $4 \times 4$ Gaussian elimination:

$$(\mathbf{T}_A^B)^{-1} = \mathbf{T}_B^A = \begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{R}_A^B)^T & -(\mathbf{R}_A^B)^T \mathbf{p}_A^B \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

### Quaternions for Singularity-Free Rotations
While Euler angles (Roll, Pitch, Yaw) suffer from kinematic singularities (**Gimbal Lock** when pitch approaches $\pm 90^\circ$, causing division by zero in coordinate transformations), unit quaternions provide a continuous, computationally robust 4-parameter representation:

$$\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} w \\ x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta / 2) \\ \mathbf{u} \sin(\theta / 2) \end{bmatrix}, \quad \|\mathbf{q}\|_2 = w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$$

where $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the unit rotation axis and $\theta$ is the rotation angle.

The **Hamilton Quaternion Product** ($\mathbf{q}_c = \mathbf{q}_a \otimes \mathbf{q}_b$) compounds successive 3D rotations:

$$\mathbf{q}_a \otimes \mathbf{q}_b = \begin{bmatrix}
w_a w_b - x_a x_b - y_a y_b - z_a z_b \\
w_a x_b + x_a w_b + y_a z_b - z_a y_b \\
w_a y_b - x_a z_b + y_a w_b + z_a x_b \\
w_a z_b + x_a y_b - y_a x_b + z_a w_b
\end{bmatrix}$$

### Lie Algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ and Tangent Space Integration
In high-frequency control loops ($1000\text{ Hz}$), velocities are expressed as continuous **spatial twists** $\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ combining linear velocity $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3$:

$$\boldsymbol{\xi} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ \boldsymbol{\omega} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^6$$

The wedge operator $(\cdot)^\wedge$ maps $\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ to the matrix Lie algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$:

$$\boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge = \begin{bmatrix} [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times & \mathbf{v} \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, \quad \text{where } [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_z & \omega_y \\ \omega_z & 0 & -\omega_x \\ -\omega_y & \omega_x & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Integrating a constant twist $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ over a discrete time step $\Delta t$ updates the robot pose without numerical distortion using the **Exponential Map**:

$$\mathbf{T}(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{T}(t) \cdot \exp\left( \boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge \Delta t \right)$$

where $\exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge \Delta t)$ is computed via Rodrigues' rotation formula:

$$\exp([\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times \Delta t) = \mathbf{I}_{3 \times 3} + \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\theta}[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times + \frac{1 - \cos(\theta)}{\theta^2}[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times^2, \quad \theta = \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| \Delta t$$

```c
// Normalizing quaternion to prevent floating-point drift in 1 kHz ISR
void quaternion_normalize(float q[4]) {
    float norm_sq = q[0]*q[0] + q[1]*q[1] + q[2]*q[2] + q[3]*q[3];
    if (norm_sq > 1e-12f) {
        float inv_norm = 1.0f / sqrtf(norm_sq);
        q[0] *= inv_norm; q[1] *= inv_norm; q[2] *= inv_norm; q[3] *= inv_norm;
    } else {
        q[0] = 1.0f; q[1] = 0.0f; q[2] = 0.0f; q[3] = 0.0f; // Identity fallback
    }
}
```

## 3. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) & Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programs

### Forward Invariance and Nagumo's Theorem
Consider a control-affine physical dynamical system:

$$\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$$

where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the physical state (positions, velocities), $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the control input (motor torques, voltages), and $f, g$ describe the unforced drift physics and control input dynamics.

A physical safety envelope is defined as the 0-superlevel set of a continuously differentiable scalar function $h(\mathbf{x}): \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$:

$$\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \}$$

$$\partial \mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid h(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \} \quad (\text{Safety Boundary})$$

$$\text{Int}(\mathcal{C}) = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid h(\mathbf{x}) > 0 \} \quad (\text{Safe Interior})$$

The set $\mathcal{C}$ is **forward invariant** if for every initial state $\mathbf{x}(0) \in \mathcal{C}$, the trajectory remains safe for all future time: $\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{C}, \forall t \ge 0$.

By Nagumo's theorem, forward invariance holds if and only if the time derivative of $h(\mathbf{x})$ satisfies:

$$\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) \ge -\alpha(h(\mathbf{x}))$$

where $\alpha(\cdot)$ is an **extended class-$\mathcal{K}$ function** (strictly increasing, $\alpha(0) = 0$, typically chosen as linear $\alpha(h) = \gamma h$ with $\gamma > 0$).

### Lie Derivatives and Affine Control Invariants
Expanding $\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})$ via the chain rule:

$$\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot [f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}] = \underbrace{\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) f(\mathbf{x})}_{L_f h(\mathbf{x})} + \underbrace{\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) g(\mathbf{x})}_{L_g h(\mathbf{x})} \mathbf{u}$$

* **$L_f h(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}$:** The *Lie derivative along $f$*, representing the natural physical rate of change of safety clearance under zero actuator power (momentum drift).
* **$L_g h(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times m}$:** The *Lie derivative along $g$*, representing the control authority over safety clearance.

The barrier condition becomes an **affine linear inequality** in the control input $\mathbf{u}$:

$$L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$$

* **Intuition:** When far inside the safe set ($h(\mathbf{x}) \gg 0$), $-\gamma h(\mathbf{x})$ is a large negative number, imposing zero restriction on performance. As the state approaches the boundary ($h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$), $-\gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$, forcing $\dot{h} \ge 0$ and repelling the state back into the safe interior.

```
       h(x) >> 0 (Safe Interior)                 h(x) -> 0 (Boundary)
  ---------------------------------       ---------------------------------
  dh/dt >= -gamma * h (Permissive)        dh/dt >= 0 (Zero Approach Speed)
  Actuator full authority                Braking / Repulsion enforced
```

### The Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Program (CBF-QP)
In the Proposal–Permission architecture, upstream neural policies (System 2 / System 1.5) emit candidate torque proposals $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$. The bare-metal microcontroller (System 1) solves the following convex Quadratic Program at $1000\text{ Hz}$:

$$\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} \frac{1}{2} \| \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \|_{\mathbf{W}}^2$$

$$\text{subject to:} \quad L_f h_i(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0, \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, M$$

$$\mathbf{u}_{\text{min}} \le \mathbf{u} \le \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}}$$

* **Minimal Intervention Principle:** If $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ satisfies all barrier inequalities, the objective is minimized at $\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$, passing the neural policy's action with zero modification. If $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ violates a barrier, the QP executes an orthogonal projection onto the safe half-space boundary $\partial \mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$, modifying the command by the minimum mathematical perturbation required to preserve invariance.

## 4. Discrete State Estimation & Covariance Mechanics (Continuous-Discrete EKF)

Physical AI pipelines fuse high-rate ($1000\text{ Hz}$) noisy proprioceptive inertial measurements with delayed, multi-modal exteroceptive observations ($10\text{--}30\text{ Hz}$) using the **Continuous-Discrete Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)**.

### Continuous Physics Propagation (IMU Prediction)
Between measurement arrivals, state dynamics evolve continuously:

$$\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = f(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{u}(t)) + \mathbf{w}(t), \quad \mathbf{w}(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_c)$$

Discretizing over integration step $\Delta t = 1.0\text{ ms}$:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1} + f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}, \mathbf{u}_{k-1}) \Delta t$$

$$\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} = \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1} \mathbf{F}_k^T + \mathbf{Q}_d$$

where:
* $\mathbf{F}_k \approx \mathbf{I} + \left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1}} \Delta t$ is the state transition Jacobian.
* $\mathbf{Q}_d \approx \mathbf{Q}_c \Delta t$ is the discrete process noise covariance.

### Discrete Measurement Update & Outlier Rejection
When an exteroceptive measurement $\mathbf{z}_k \in \mathbb{R}^m$ arrives from vision or LiDAR:

$$\mathbf{z}_k = h(\mathbf{x}_k) + \mathbf{v}_k, \quad \mathbf{v}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_k)$$

1. **Innovation Residual:** $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k = \mathbf{z}_k - h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1})$
2. **Innovation Covariance:** $\mathbf{S}_k = \mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k$, where $\mathbf{H}_k = \left. \frac{\partial h}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}}$
3. **Mahalanobis Innovation Gating:** To reject optical reflections and sensor glitches, test the squared Mahalanobis distance against the Chi-Square distribution $\chi_{m, 1-\alpha}^2$:

$$d_M^2 = \tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k^T \mathbf{S}_k^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k \le \chi_{m, 1-\alpha}^2$$

If $d_M^2 > \chi_{\text{threshold}}^2$, the measurement is discarded as an un-modeled artifact.

4. **Kalman Gain Computation:** $\mathbf{K}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{S}_k^{-1}$
5. **State Update:** $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k \tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k$
6. **Joseph-Form Covariance Update (Numerical Stability):** On fixed-point and single-precision embedded silicon, the standard covariance update $\mathbf{P} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}$ suffers from round-off errors that destroy symmetry and positive semi-definiteness. Embedded firmware must enforce the **Joseph stabilized form**:

$$\mathbf{P}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k) \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T + \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{K}_k^T$$

Because both terms are quadratic forms $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{A}^T$, positive semi-definiteness ($\mathbf{P} \succeq 0$) is mathematically guaranteed regardless of numerical precision.

## 5. Field-Oriented Control (FOC) and Space-Vector Modulation

To translate high-level torque commands into physical electromagnetic forces, brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motors (PMSM) rely on **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)** executing in dedicated hardware timer peripherals at $20\text{ kHz}$ ($\Delta t = 50\,\mu\text{s}$).

### Clarke Transformation ($abc \to \alpha\beta$)
Transforms balanced three-phase stator currents $(i_a, i_b, i_c)$ into a stationary two-phase orthogonal coordinate system:

$$\begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix} = \frac{2}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_a \\ i_b \\ i_c \end{bmatrix}$$

Using the zero-sum property $i_a + i_b + i_c = 0$, this simplifies to:

$$i_\alpha = i_a, \quad i_\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} (i_a + 2 i_b)$$

### Park Transformation ($\alpha\beta \to dq$)
Rotates the stationary $(\alpha, \beta)$ currents into the rotor's rotating reference frame using the electrical rotor angle $\theta_e = P \cdot \theta_{\text{mech}}$ (where $P$ is the motor pole-pair count):

$$\begin{bmatrix} i_d \\ i_q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_e & \sin\theta_e \\ -\sin\theta_e & \cos\theta_e \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix}$$

* **Direct-Axis Current ($i_d$):** Aligns parallel with the rotor permanent magnet flux. Setting $i_d^* = 0$ eliminates wasteful radial forces and maximizes electrical efficiency.
* **Quadrature-Axis Current ($i_q$):** Aligns $90^\circ$ electrical ahead of rotor flux, producing pure orthogonal electromagnetic torque:

$$\tau_{\text{motor}} = \frac{3}{2} P \lambda_{\text{pm}} i_q = K_t \cdot i_q$$

where $\lambda_{\text{pm}}$ is the permanent magnet flux linkage ($\text{Wb}$) and $K_t$ is the motor torque constant ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m/A}$).

### $I^2t$ Thermal Accumulator
To prevent motor stator insulation breakdown ($T > 155^\circ\text{C}$), the motor driver integrates Joulean thermal dissipation in real time:

$$E_{\text{thermal}}(t) = \int_0^t I_{\text{phase}}^2(\tau) R_{\text{stator}} \, d\tau$$

When $E_{\text{thermal}}$ exceeds the continuous thermal rating $E_{\text{continuous}}$, the controller linearly derates peak torque current $i_q^{\text{limit}} \leftarrow i_q^{\text{nominal}} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{T_j - 85^\circ\text{C}}{155^\circ\text{C} - 85^\circ\text{C}}\right)$.

## 6. Frequency-Domain Stability and Sampled-Data Phase Margin

In classical digital control, converting continuous commands to discrete hardware outputs introduces uncompensated phase lag that erodes the system's stability margin.

### Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) Phase Lag
A digital-to-analog converter holding a commanded setpoint constant over sample period $T$ is modeled by the Zero-Order Hold transfer function:

$$G_{\text{ZOH}}(s) = \frac{1 - e^{-sT}}{s}$$

Evaluating its frequency response $s = j\omega$:

$$G_{\text{ZOH}}(j\omega) = T \cdot \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega T}{2}\right) e^{-j \frac{\omega T}{2}}$$

The magnitude attenuation is $\left| \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega T}{2}\right) \right|$, while the **exact phase lag** is:

$$\Delta \phi_{\text{ZOH}} = -\frac{\omega T}{2} \quad (\text{radians}) = -\omega \cdot \frac{T}{2} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} \quad (\text{degrees})$$

### The Phase Margin Stability Criterion
Let $\omega_c$ be the open-loop gain crossover frequency ($\|G(j\omega_c)\| = 1$) of the physical mechanism, and $\text{PM}_{\text{nominal}}$ be the nominal phase margin. Total sensorimotor transport delay $\tau_{\text{delay}} = \tau_{\text{compute}} + \frac{1}{2} T_{\text{sample}}$ introduces phase lag:

$$\Delta \phi = -\omega_c \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$$

The effective closed-loop phase margin is:

$$\text{PM}_{\text{effective}} = \text{PM}_{\text{nominal}} - \omega_c \tau_{\text{delay}} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$$

* **Stability Limit:** If $\tau_{\text{delay}} \ge \frac{\text{PM}_{\text{nominal}}}{\omega_c} \cdot \frac{\pi}{180^\circ}$, then $\text{PM}_{\text{effective}} \le 0^\circ$. Stabilizing negative feedback flips into positive feedback, triggering explosive limit-cycle oscillations.

| Sample Frequency ($f_s$) | Sample Period ($T$) | ZOH Delay ($\tau_d = T/2$) | Phase Lag at $\omega_c = 25\text{ rad/s}$ ($4\text{ Hz}$) | Impact on $35^\circ$ Phase Margin |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **$10\text{ Hz}$** (Slow VLM) | $100\text{ ms}$ | $50\text{ ms}$ | **$-71.6^\circ$** | **$-36.6^\circ$ (Destructive Instability / Crash)** |
| **$50\text{ Hz}$** (Action Chunk) | $20\text{ ms}$ | $10\text{ ms}$ | **$-14.3^\circ$** | **$+20.7^\circ$ (Reduced Damping, Mild Overshoot)** |
| **$1000\text{ Hz}$** (MCU Reflex) | $1.0\text{ ms}$ | $0.5\text{ ms}$ | **$-0.72^\circ$** | **$+34.3^\circ$ (Robust Closed-Loop Stability)** |

## 8. Pinhole Camera Geometry, Optical Unprojection, and Epipolar Invariants

In physical perception, an optical camera does not produce 3D coordinates directly. It captures a 2D projection of 3D Euclidean space onto a semiconductor photodiode grid. To transform pixel observations into metric affordance tokens in $SE(3)$ that an actuator can reach, systems rely on calibrated projective geometry, depth unprojection, and epipolar multi-view constraints.

### The Pinhole Projection Model & Intrinsic Matrix $\mathbf{K}$

Consider a 3D point $\mathbf{P}_C = [X_C, Y_C, Z_C]^T \in \mathbb{R}^3$ in the camera optical reference frame, where the $+Z_C$ axis points forward along the optical axis, $+X_C$ points to the right, and $+Y_C$ points downward. Under ideal perspective projection, light rays pass through the optical center (pinhole aperture) and project onto the image sensor plane at focal distance $f$:

$$\tilde{x} = \frac{X_C}{Z_C}, \quad \tilde{y} = \frac{Y_C}{Z_C}$$

where $(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y})$ are dimensionless normalized image plane coordinates.

To convert normalized coordinates into discrete sensor pixel indices $(u, v)$, the optical projection is parameterized by the **Camera Intrinsic Matrix** $\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$:

$$\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} f_x & s & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

where:
* $f_x = \frac{f}{p_w}, \; f_y = \frac{f}{p_h}$: Effective focal lengths expressed in pixel units, where $p_w, p_h$ are the physical horizontal and vertical pixel pitches ($\mu\text{m/pixel}$) on the CMOS silicon die.
* $(c_x, c_y)$: Pixel coordinates of the **principal point** (the intersection of the optical axis with the sensor array, ideally $(W/2, H/2)$).
* $s$: Pixel grid skew coefficient (identically zero, $s = 0$, for modern lithographic rectangular silicon sensors).

Under zero skew ($s=0$), the projective mapping from a 3D camera point $\mathbf{P}_C$ to homogeneous pixel coordinates $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = [u, v, 1]^T$ is:

$$Z_C \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{P}_C = \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X_C \\ Y_C \\ Z_C \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f_x X_C + c_x Z_C \\ f_y Y_C + c_y Z_C \\ Z_C \end{bmatrix}$$

Expanding into inhomogeneous Cartesian pixel coordinates:

$$u = f_x \frac{X_C}{Z_C} + c_x, \qquad v = f_y \frac{Y_C}{Z_C} + c_y$$

### Optical Ray Unprojection and Metric Cartesian Coordinates

Because prospective projection collapses 3D rays onto a 2D plane, a single pixel coordinate $(u, v)$ defines an infinite angular ray rather than a discrete physical location. Recovering the 3D metric coordinate requires unprojecting along the ray using registered orthogonal depth $Z = d(u, v) \in \mathbb{R}^+$ (measured via active stereo, structured light, or time-of-flight).

The upper-triangular intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ has a direct closed-form inverse:

$$\mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{f_x} & 0 & -\frac{c_x}{f_x} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{f_y} & -\frac{c_y}{f_y} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Multiplying the homogeneous pixel vector by $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$ reconstructs the normalized unit-depth ray vector $\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}}$ in the camera optical frame:

$$\mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}} = \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{u - c_x}{f_x} \\ \frac{v - c_y}{f_y} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Scaling this ray vector by the registered depth $Z = d(u, v)$ yields the 3D metric position $\mathbf{P}_C$ in the camera optical frame:

$$\mathbf{P}_C = Z \cdot \mathbf{r}_{\text{cam}} = \begin{bmatrix} X_C \\ Y_C \\ Z_C \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{u - c_x}{f_x} Z \\ \frac{v - c_y}{f_y} Z \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

### Rigid Extrinsic Transform to Robot Base Frame

To enable physical manipulation, navigation, or obstacle avoidance, the camera-frame point $\mathbf{P}_C$ must be transformed into the robot's stationary physical base frame $B$. Applying the extrinsic homogeneous transformation matrix $\mathbf{T}_C^B = (\mathbf{R}_C^B, \mathbf{p}_C^B) \in SE(3)$:

$$\mathbf{P}_B = \mathbf{R}_C^B \mathbf{P}_C + \mathbf{p}_C^B = \mathbf{R}_C^B \left( Z \cdot \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) + \mathbf{p}_C^B$$

where $\mathbf{R}_C^B \in SO(3)$ is the $3 \times 3$ rotation matrix aligning the camera optical axes to the robot base coordinate axes, and $\mathbf{p}_C^B \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the physical lever-arm displacement vector from the base origin to the optical center.

### Surface Normal Estimation from Discrete Depth Gradients

For robotic grasping and contact mechanics, the agent requires the outward unit surface normal vector $\hat{\mathbf{n}} \in \mathbb{S}^2$ at the contact target. Considering unprojected points $\mathbf{P}_B(u, v)$ as a 2D parameterized surface, the tangent vectors spanning the local contact plane are given by spatial partial derivatives:

$$\mathbf{t}_u = \frac{\partial \mathbf{P}_B}{\partial u} \approx \frac{\mathbf{P}_B(u + \Delta u, v) - \mathbf{P}_B(u - \Delta u, v)}{2 \Delta u}$$

$$\mathbf{t}_v = \frac{\partial \mathbf{P}_B}{\partial v} \approx \frac{\mathbf{P}_B(u, v + \Delta v) - \mathbf{P}_B(u, v - \Delta v)}{2 \Delta v}$$

The outward unit normal vector $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ facing the robot sensor is computed via the normalized vector cross-product:

$$\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{t}_v \times \mathbf{t}_u}{\|\mathbf{t}_v \times \mathbf{t}_u\|_2} \in \mathbb{S}^2$$

### Multi-View Epipolar Geometry and Sampson Residual Metric

When fusing multi-camera observations or tracking stereo visual odometry, corresponding pixel points across two calibrated viewpoints must satisfy geometric coplanarity.

Let $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be a physical 3D scene point observed by Camera 1 as $\mathbf{P}_1$ and by Camera 2 as $\mathbf{P}_2$. The two cameras are related by relative rigid-body rotation $\mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$ and baseline translation $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, such that $\mathbf{P}_2 = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1 + \mathbf{t}$.

The vectors $\mathbf{P}_2$, $\mathbf{t}$, and $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P}_1$ are coplanar. Expressing this geometric condition as a scalar triple product:

$$\mathbf{P}_2^T \left( \mathbf{t} \times (\mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1) \right) = 0 \implies \mathbf{P}_2^T [\mathbf{t}]_\times \mathbf{R} \mathbf{P}_1 = 0$$

Defining the **Essential Matrix** $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$:

$$\mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{t}]_\times \mathbf{R}$$

Substituting the normalized image coordinates $\mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{K}_1^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{K}_2^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2$ defines the **Fundamental Matrix** $\mathbf{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2^T \mathbf{F} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}_2^{-T} \mathbf{E} \mathbf{K}_1^{-1} = \mathbf{K}_2^{-T} [\mathbf{t}]_\times \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}_1^{-1}$$

* **Epipolar Line Invariant:** A pixel point $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1$ in Camera 1 defines an epipolar line $\mathbf{l}_2 = \mathbf{F} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1$ in Camera 2 upon which the corresponding point $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2$ must lie: $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2^T \mathbf{l}_2 = 0$.

During active robot operation, mechanical shocks and thermal expansion degrade camera extrinsic parameters. To quantify geometric consistency without re-triangulating 3D points, the online calibration filter computes the **Sampson Epipolar Error** $\epsilon_{\text{Sampson}}$ (the first-order geometric distance approximation from the points to their respective epipolar lines):

$$\epsilon_{\text{Sampson}}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1, \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2) = \frac{(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2^T \mathbf{F} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1)^2}{(\mathbf{F}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1)_1^2 + (\mathbf{F}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1)_2^2 + (\mathbf{F}^T\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2)_1^2 + (\mathbf{F}^T\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_2)_2^2}$$

where $(\mathbf{v})_i$ denotes the $i$-th element of vector $\mathbf{v}$. If $\epsilon_{\text{Sampson}} > \epsilon_{\text{threshold}}$ across tracked feature pairs, the estimator flags extrinsic baseline drift and triggers real-time bundle adjustment.

### Thermal Baseline Expansion and Triangulation Error Sensitivity

In stereo perception, metric depth $Z$ is triangulated from stereo disparity $d = u_1 - u_2$ across physical baseline $b = \|\mathbf{t}\|$:

$$Z = \frac{f \cdot b}{d}$$

Differentiating with respect to disparity $d$ and baseline length $b$:

$$\delta Z = \frac{\partial Z}{\partial d} \delta d + \frac{\partial Z}{\partial b} \delta b = -\frac{f \cdot b}{d^2} \delta d + \frac{f}{d} \delta b = -\frac{Z^2}{f \cdot b} \delta d + \frac{Z}{b} \delta b$$

* **Quadratic Distance Sensitivity:** Triangulation depth uncertainty grows quadratically ($\propto Z^2$) with distance. At short ranges ($Z=0.5\text{ m}$), a $0.5\text{ px}$ disparity noise induces millimeter error; at far ranges ($Z=5.0\text{ m}$), the exact same noise induces tens of centimeters of spatial uncertainty.

Chassis aluminum expands under operational temperature rise $\Delta T$ with thermal coefficient $\alpha_{\text{Al}} \approx 23 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$:

$$\delta b = b_0 \cdot \alpha_{\text{Al}} \cdot \Delta T$$

Additionally, uneven thermal expansion or motor torque vibration induces an angular baseline tilt $\delta \theta$, shifting feature disparity by $\delta d_{\text{tilt}} = f \cdot \tan(\delta \theta) \approx f \cdot \delta \theta$. The resulting depth error is:

$$\delta Z_{\text{tilt}} \approx -\frac{Z^2}{b} \delta \theta$$

For a stereo camera with baseline $b = 0.20\text{ m}$, an angular deflection of just $\delta \theta = 0.5^\circ = 0.00873\text{ rad}$ produces:
* At working distance $Z = 1.0\text{ m}$: $\delta Z = \frac{1.0^2}{0.20} \times 0.00873 = 0.0436\text{ m} \approx 4.4\text{ cm}$.
* At obstacle distance $Z = 5.0\text{ m}$: $\delta Z = \frac{5.0^2}{0.20} \times 0.00873 = 1.091\text{ m} \approx 109.1\text{ cm}$.

This reveals why static calibration matrices fail in physical deployment and mandates continuous online epipolar tracking.

### Embedded C Implementation (`malloc = 0`)

The following C implementation executes in $< 0.4\,\mu\text{s}$ per query on an ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller, unprojecting a 2D depth pixel into a metric 3D base coordinate and estimating the contact surface normal in static SRAM:

```c
#include <math.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef struct {
    float fx_inv, fy_inv;   // 1.0f / fx, 1.0f / fy
    float cx, cy;           // Principal optical center
    float R_cam_to_base[3][3]; // Extrinsic rotation matrix
    float p_cam_to_base[3];    // Extrinsic translation vector (meters)
} camera_intrinsics_extrinsics_t;

// Fast unprojection from pixel (u,v) + depth (Z) to 3D Base Frame PB
void unproject_pixel_to_base(
    float u, float v, float depth_m,
    const camera_intrinsics_extrinsics_t* calib,
    float p_base_out[3]
) {
    // 1. Reconstruct 3D camera coordinates PC
    float x_c = (u - calib->cx) * calib->fx_inv * depth_m;
    float y_c = (v - calib->cy) * calib->fy_inv * depth_m;
    float z_c = depth_m;

    // 2. Transform to Robot Base Frame: PB = R * PC + p
    p_base_out[0] = calib->R_cam_to_base[0][0]*x_c + calib->R_cam_to_base[0][1]*y_c + calib->R_cam_to_base[0][2]*z_c + calib->p_cam_to_base[0];
    p_base_out[1] = calib->R_cam_to_base[1][0]*x_c + calib->R_cam_to_base[1][1]*y_c + calib->R_cam_to_base[1][2]*z_c + calib->p_cam_to_base[1];
    p_base_out[2] = calib->R_cam_to_base[2][0]*x_c + calib->R_cam_to_base[2][1]*y_c + calib->R_cam_to_base[2][2]*z_c + calib->p_cam_to_base[2];
}

// Compute unit surface normal from 3 unprojected neighbor points in Base Frame
bool compute_surface_normal(
    const float p_center[3], const float p_right[3], const float p_down[3],
    float normal_out[3]
) {
    // Tangent vectors: tu = p_right - p_center, tv = p_down - p_center
    float tu[3] = { p_right[0] - p_center[0], p_right[1] - p_center[1], p_right[2] - p_center[2] };
    float tv[3] = { p_down[0] - p_center[0],  p_down[1] - p_center[1],  p_down[2] - p_center[2] };

    // Cross product: n = tv x tu
    float nx = tv[1]*tu[2] - tv[2]*tu[1];
    float ny = tv[2]*tu[0] - tv[0]*tu[2];
    float nz = tv[0]*tu[1] - tv[1]*tu[0];

    float norm_sq = nx*nx + ny*ny + nz*nz;
    if (norm_sq < 1e-8f) {
        normal_out[0] = 0.0f; normal_out[1] = 0.0f; normal_out[2] = 1.0f; // Default upward
        return false;
    }
    float inv_norm = 1.0f / sqrtf(norm_sq);
    normal_out[0] = nx * inv_norm;
    normal_out[1] = ny * inv_norm;
    normal_out[2] = nz * inv_norm;
    return true;
}
```
